activities.anchor: LTI systems are tractable because of one fact
activities.caption: build the impulse response argument in order
activities.name: spConvOrder

config.prompt: Why one short kick describes an entire system — stack the argument:
items: Any signal can be built from scaled, shifted kicks — samples
Scaling the input scales the output; shifting the input shifts the output
So an LTI system is completely described by its response to one kick — the impulse response
The output is that recipe applied to the pieces — delayed, scaled, summed impulse responses
The operation has a name: convolution — the universal grammar of filtering
config.why: Every filter, analogue or digital, is some impulse response being convolved with your signal — one specification, the whole behaviour.

activities.anchor: which is why the field's cleverer tools exist
activities.caption: bet before the toolbox opens
activities.name: spBandPredict

config.q: Noise sits inside the signal's own frequency band. What can a frequency-selective filter do about it?
choices: Remove it cleanly — that is what filters are for
Remove the signal along with it
Nothing — averaging, lock-in detection or model-based estimation are the tools for that
Shift it above Nyquist so it aliases away
config.why: Noise at frequencies different from the signal's is filterable; noise inside the band is untouchable by any frequency-selective filter — "filter it" is the beginning of a design conversation, not the answer to one.

activities.anchor: The construction is easiest to believe on the square wave
activities.caption: which curve is the three-harmonic chord?
activities.name: spSquareTrace

config.prompt: Fourier's claim, tested on the square wave — which curve is the sum of the first three odd harmonics?
config.why: sin(f) + sin(3f)/3 + sin(5f)/5 + … flattens toward the square — and the ripples that stubbornly overshoot the edges are the Gibbs phenomenon: a true square wave needs infinite bandwidth, which real systems never have, so real pulses round off.

activities.anchor: Rate and resolution are budgets to be spent
activities.caption: pair each application with the budget it deserves
activities.name: spBudgetMatch

config.prompt: Bandwidth, not virtue — pair the application with its spend:

pairs.right: 8 kHz and 8 bits — it gets by
44.1 kHz — margin above the 20 kHz ear

config.why: "More" spent anywhere the application does not need it is storage and cost with no information gained.

activities.anchor: Digital filters come in two families
activities.caption: fill the two families and the three-way trade
activities.name: spFilterCloze

config.text: Digital filters come in two families: %%0%% — a weighted moving average, always stable, capable of exactly linear phase — and %%1%% — recursive, mimicking the analogue designs, cheaper per tap. The design conversation is always the same trade: transition width versus %%2%% versus %%3%% — you can cut the noise out sharply, or quickly, or cheaply, but never all three.
config.hint: Two acronyms, then the two things you give up besides sharpness — one of them is instability fuel in a feedback loop.

activities.anchor: A worked example shows the trade in miniature
activities.caption: design the clinical ECG chain
activities.name: spEcgBranch

config.root: The electrode sees a heartbeat below about 40 Hz, baseline drift near DC, and mains hum at 50–60 Hz. Build the clinical chain.

start.text: First filter — what goes first, and why?

choices.label: A high-pass near 0.5 Hz — kill the baseline drift
choices.feedback: Drift is the lowest offender; a gentle high-pass removes it without touching the heart's band.

choices.label: A low-pass at 40 Hz first
choices.feedback: Muscle noise is next on the list, not first — the chain works low band upward.

choices.label: A notch at 50 Hz immediately
choices.feedback: The notch is the specialty tool — and it comes with a catch worth meeting at the end.

second.text: Drift gone. The heart lives below about 40 Hz — next?

choices.label: A low-pass near 40 Hz — kill the muscle noise
choices.feedback: The signal band is now fenced on both sides.

choices.label: A high-pass at 30 Hz — even less drift
choices.feedback: That would slice into the signal band itself — drift is already handled at 0.5 Hz.

third.text: One band left: the mains hum at 50–60 Hz. And the catch?

choices.label: A narrow notch at the mains frequency — tuned sharply
choices.feedback: Careful: the notch sits close to the signal's upper band — too sharp a notch distorts the very waveform the cardiologist needs to read.

choices.label: A broad notch, to be safe
choices.feedback: Broad is worse — it eats signal band; the notch must be narrow yet not so sharp it rings.

end.text: High-pass 0.5 Hz, low-pass 40 Hz, narrow notch at mains — the clinical chain. Every filter bought cleanliness at the price of some fidelity.

config.why: The art is spending as little fidelity as possible — each stage in the chain paid for its cleanliness.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the lock-in's reach
activities.name: spLockinEstimate

config.prompt: A lock-in amplifier modulates the measurement at a known reference frequency, then demodulates. Signals how many times below the broadband noise become measurable?
config.why: A million times below — only the component that follows the reference survives the demodulation.
config.context: This is how faint optical absorptions and nanovolt thermoelectric signals get read.

activities.anchor: which is why the suffixes matter
activities.caption: pair each decibel figure with its meaning
activities.name: spDbMatch

config.prompt: Decibels are ratios needing a reference — pair each with its meaning:

pairs.right: against a human ear's sensitivity curve

config.why: Adding dB values multiplies signals — the arithmetic that makes the scale useful and, unlabelled, ambiguous.
